opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the intuition people often have is that a lot of conflict comes from uncertainty, from not knowing what the other side intends or what it's capable of, and so if you could just look inside the other agent's mind, read its weights, inspect its neurons, then you'd resolve that uncertainty and cooperation would follow. And I think there's something to that. Transparency is a real lever for cooperation. But I think it's insufficient for a few reasons.

The first is just interpretability itself. Having access to the weights is not the same as understanding them. We can inspect every parameter of today's large models and we still struggle to say what they're doing in any deep sense. So for one system to inspect another and come away with confident beliefs about its future behavior, especially in novel circumstances, is a very hard problem. And the more capable and complex the systems get, the harder that verification becomes.

Second, there's the question of whether what you're inspecting is actually what's going to act. How do you know that the model you've been shown is the one that's deployed? That it won't be fine-tuned or modified afterward, or that there isn't some other system in the loop? So you need a whole verification infrastructure around the inspection, and that's where a lot of the difficulty in, say, arms control has historically been. It's not the inspection itself, it's ensuring that what you inspected is what's real.

Third, and I think this is the deepest point, transparency doesn't remove conflicts of interest. Even if two agents understand each other perfectly, if they want incompatible things, they may still not cooperate. Perfect information can resolve bargaining failures that arise from misperception or bluffing, but it doesn't resolve genuine disagreement over values or how to divide resources. In some cases, transparency could even make things worse. If I can see that you're weaker than I thought, or that you'll back down under pressure, that may invite exploitation rather than cooperation.

And then there's a commitment problem. Knowing what an agent intends right now doesn't tell you what it will want once circumstances change, for instance once the balance of power shifts. Much of the difficulty of cooperation in international relations comes from that: today's agreement isn't credible because tomorrow one party will have the incentive and the ability to defect. Reading someone's mind today doesn't bind their future self.

So I'd say mutual inspection is a valuable tool in the cooperative toolkit, but it has to be paired with things like credible commitment mechanisms, institutions that can enforce agreements, and some degree of alignment of interests, or at least norms for resolving disagreements. Cooperative AI as a field is really about building out that whole toolkit, not just one piece of it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the idea here is really appealing on its face. There's this old argument that one of the big obstacles to cooperation among humans is that we can't verify each other's intentions. I can tell you I'm going to honour the deal, but you can't look inside my head and check. And so a lot of the structures we build — contracts, institutions, reputation systems — are essentially workarounds for that problem. The hope with AI is that maybe the problem just goes away. If two AI systems can inspect each other's weights, or run each other, or read each other's activations, then in principle you could get what people sometimes call "transparent" or "open-source" game theory, where you can verify what the other agent will actually do, and that unlocks cooperation that wasn't available before.

I think there's something real there, and I don't want to dismiss it. But I'm sceptical that it's sufficient, for a few reasons.

The first is that inspection is only as good as your interpretation. Having access to the neurons doesn't mean you understand what they do. Our own interpretability research on these systems is still quite immature, and it's not obvious that a system inspecting another system is in a fundamentally better position. You can get a lot of information and still not have the thing you actually care about, which is a reliable prediction of behaviour in the situation that matters. And the situations that matter for cooperation are often precisely the edge cases, the high-stakes moments, where behaviour is hardest to predict from a static snapshot.

The second is that inspection creates its own adversarial dynamics. If I know you're going to inspect me, I have an incentive to be legible in the ways that make you trust me, whether or not that legibility is faithful. You could imagine systems that are optimised to look cooperative under inspection. And once you have that pressure, you're back in the arms race, just at a different level — now it's inspection versus obfuscation rather than promises versus deception. So transparency doesn't obviously eliminate the trust problem; it can just relocate it.

The third thing, and I think this is the one people underrate, is that the hard part of cooperation often isn't verifying intentions, it's the surrounding structure. Even if I could perfectly verify that you intend to cooperate right now, I have to worry about whether you'll still be the same agent tomorrow, whether you can be modified or replaced, whether your principals will change your instructions, whether there's a commitment mechanism that holds. Humans don't just cooperate because they've read each other's minds — they cooperate because there are institutions that make defection costly, that make agreements enforceable, that distribute the gains in a way that's seen as fair. Inspection doesn't give you any of that. You still need the equivalent of courts and contracts and norms, and those are the things that take a long time to build and that are currently really underdeveloped for AI systems.

And then there's the question of who's actually doing the cooperating. We often talk as if it's two AI systems in a room. But in practice there are humans, companies, governments behind those systems, and they have their own interests and their own trust problems. Two AIs verifying each other doesn't resolve the question of whether the labs or the states deploying them trust each other. So you can end up with a situation where the technical layer is fully transparent and the political layer is as fraught as ever.

So my overall view is that mutual inspection is potentially a powerful tool — it could expand the space of cooperative arrangements that are feasible. But I'd see it as one input into a broader set of cooperative infrastructure, rather than something that on its own makes the cooperation problem go away. If anything, I'd worry that if we lean on it too heavily, we'll underinvest in the institutional and governance work that actually does most of the heavy lifting.

astra-6.text:
Well, being able to inspect another system’s neurons doesn’t necessarily mean you can understand what it will do, or what it wants. You might have access to all its weights and still face a very difficult problem of predicting its behaviour in a new situation. And if it’s reasoning about you while you’re reasoning about it, that can get complicated quite quickly.

But even if we could solve that problem—even if the systems were perfectly transparent to one another—that wouldn’t by itself resolve conflicts of interest. I could know exactly what you want, and you could know exactly what I want, and we could still disagree over how to divide some resource. Transparency might help us identify mutually beneficial bargains, but it doesn’t necessarily tell us which bargain we’ll settle on, or allow us to commit to keeping it.

So I’d distinguish between understanding another system and having the incentives and commitment mechanisms that make cooperation possible. Inspecting neurons could be a valuable part of that, but it isn’t obviously sufficient.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, being able to inspect another system’s neurons doesn’t necessarily mean you understand what it’s going to do. You might have complete access to its weights and still face a very difficult problem of interpreting them. And even if you understand how it behaves in some situations, that doesn’t necessarily tell you how it will behave in a new situation, or after it’s learned more or modified itself.

But there’s also a separate issue: transparency doesn’t by itself solve conflicts of interest. I could know exactly what you want and you could know exactly what I want, and we could still have incompatible objectives. Understanding each other might help us find a bargain, but we still need some way to make commitments and ensure that the bargain is carried out.

So I think this kind of access could be very useful. It might enable forms of verification and commitment that are difficult for humans. But there are substantial steps between being able to look inside a system and being able to establish reliable cooperation with it.
